claims.text: On galaxy-integrated scales, star-formation-rate surface density follows a super-linear power law of total (HI+H2) gas surface density with index N approximately 1.4, spanning normal disks and starbursts (the Schmidt-Kennicutt law).
At sub-kiloparsec resolution the star-formation rate correlates tightly with molecular gas (CO/H2) and is essentially uncorrelated with atomic HI.
Atomic-hydrogen surface density saturates near 9-10 solar masses per square parsec, and star-formation efficiency is severely suppressed in HI-dominated outer disks above that transition.
The molecular-gas depletion time in normal local disks is of order 1-2 Gyr (about 2.3 Gyr under a standard conversion factor), roughly constant within the inner molecular disk.
Star-formation rate scales approximately linearly with dense-gas (HCN) luminosity, from whole galaxies down to individual Milky Way clumps.
Molecular clouds convert gas to stars inefficiently, of order 1-2% per free-fall time, so cloud depletion times (~82 Myr) vastly exceed the free-fall (~1.4 Myr) and crossing times.
The CO-to-H2 conversion factor is not universal: it rises steeply toward low metallicity and depends on the radiation field, diverging below 12+log(O/H) approximately 8.4.
Whether star formation obeys a single super-linear total-gas law or a near-linear molecular law with distinct regimes is unresolved, since the relations differ with spatial averaging scale.
Whether mergers/starbursts occupy a separate, more efficient star-formation sequence from secular disks, or the apparent bimodality is an artifact of the CO-to-H2 conversion factor, is debated.
claims.debate_topic: Disk/starburst bimodality of the star-formation law

claims.text: Whether molecular hydrogen is physically necessary for star formation or merely co-located with shielded self-gravitating cold gas is contested; a decisive test requires very low-metallicity regimes.
claims.debate_topic: Causal role of H2 in star formation

claims.text: The comoving cosmic star-formation-rate density rises to a broad maximum near z approximately 1.9 and declines thereafter, well described by the analytic fit psi(z) = 0.015 (1+z)^2.7 / [1 + ((1+z)/2.9)^5.6].
Roughly half of today's stellar mass had formed by z approximately 1.3, about one quarter above z approximately 2, and less than about 1% at z greater than 6.
Dust-obscured star formation is a major and near-dominant contributor around cosmic noon, making far-infrared tracers essential.
The rest-frame ultraviolet luminosity functions at high redshift have steep faint-end slopes, alpha approximately -2 at z approximately 7 (measured -2.01 +/- 0.21).
The stellar-mass-density history is broadly consistent with the time-integrated star-formation-rate density once mass return is included, though a residual normalization offset persists.

The initial mass function materially sets the star-formation-rate normalization, stellar-mass return fraction (R approximately 0.27 Salpeter, 0.41 Chabrier), and net metal yield (y approximately 0.016 Salpeter, 0.032 Chabrier).

Whether the steep z greater than 6 star-formation decline is intrinsic or amplified by galaxies below the detection limit is unsettled, and whether faint galaxies supply enough ionizing photons for reionization depends on an unknown escape fraction.
claims.debate_topic: High-z decline, faint-end turnover, and reionization budget

claims.text: The observed core-collapse supernova rate falls short of the rate predicted from the integrated star-formation-rate density, an unresolved normalization tension.

sections.section: Star-Forming Main Sequence, Gas Content, and Quenching

claims.text: Star-forming galaxies occupy a tight SFR-stellar-mass main sequence with about 0.3 dex scatter that persists from z approximately 0 to 4, with normalization rising toward higher redshift.
Galaxies are bimodally distributed into a star-forming blue cloud and a quiescent red sequence, and stellar mass has built up on the red sequence since z approximately 1.
The efficiency of converting baryons into stars peaks near a halo mass of about 10^12 solar masses (~20% for L* halos) and falls on both sides.

Molecular gas fractions were high at cosmic noon (mu_gas approximately 0.3-0.5) and decline to the present, while depletion time scales with main-sequence offset as t_dep proportional to dMS^-0.44 and mu_gas proportional to dMS^+0.53.
The galaxy-integrated molecular depletion time is not constant; it varies systematically with specific star-formation rate and main-sequence offset.
Sustaining the observed star-formation history requires net gas accretion, because declining HI+H2 reservoirs cannot supply ongoing stellar-mass growth by themselves.

Whether galaxies quench by starvation/strangulation of the gas supply, rapid ejective removal, suppressed star-formation efficiency at fixed gas content, or morphological stabilization by a stellar bulge is contested.

Whether a characteristic halo mass of about 10^12 solar masses, above which virial shocks suppress cold accretion, by itself quenches massive galaxies (versus requiring AGN preventive feedback) is debated.
Whether displacement above/below the main sequence is driven mainly by gas fraction or by star-formation efficiency is unresolved.

sections.section: Mass-Metallicity Relation and the Fundamental Metallicity Relation

claims.text: Local star-forming galaxies follow a gas-phase mass-metallicity relation that rises with stellar mass, flattens above a turnover near 10^10.5 solar masses, and has about 0.1 dex scatter.
Absolute abundance calibrations disagree by up to about 0.7 dex, so mass-metallicity normalizations are comparable across studies only when the underlying scales are matched.

At fixed stellar mass, gas-phase metallicity anticorrelates with star-formation rate, and a mass-SFR-metallicity surface (the Fundamental Metallicity Relation) reduces residual scatter to about 0.05 dex locally.
Mean stellar metallicity rises with stellar mass, forming an integrated-history stellar mass-metallicity relation distinct from the gas-phase one.
The gas-phase mass-metallicity relation shifts to lower metallicity at higher redshift, with a measured decline dlog(O/H)/dz approximately -0.11 +/- 0.02 out to z approximately 3.3.
JWST/NIRSpec extends the relation to low-mass galaxies at z approximately 4-10, which are less enriched than local galaxies at fixed mass (about 0.9 dex lower at z approximately 8).

In local disks, local gas-phase metallicity correlates positively with local stellar surface mass density, and this resolved relation can reproduce aspects of the global relation and radial gradients.

Whether the Fundamental Metallicity Relation is redshift-invariant is contested: some matched analyses find no evolution to z approximately 3.3 while JWST data and simulations indicate a ~0.5 dex offset at z greater than 6 or an evolving weak secondary SFR dependence.
Whether the high-redshift low-mass MZR slope evolves is unresolved: a slope near 0.30 unchanged to z approximately 3.3 versus a shallower 0.17 +/- 0.03 at z = 3-10.

Which absolute abundance scale transfers to high redshift is unresolved, as direct-temperature and photoionization-model calibrations disagree and applying local calibrations to early galaxies can bias oxygen abundance downward by up to about 1 dex.
The mass-metallicity relation alone cannot uniquely separate the roles of metal-loaded outflows, pristine inflow, star-formation efficiency, and gas retention; models remain degenerate.
Closed-box chemical evolution fails, most sharply through the G-dwarf problem, so galaxy enrichment requires open-box gas exchange (inflow, outflow, recycling).
Two nucleosynthetic channels dominate the alpha-versus-iron pattern: core-collapse supernovae deliver prompt alpha-elements while Type Ia supernovae deliver delayed iron.

The Type Ia supernova delay-time distribution is a continuously declining power law of index approximately -1.07 from a few hundred Myr to over 10 Gyr, with a production efficiency approximately 1.3e-3 SNe Ia per solar mass formed.

Low- and intermediate-mass asymptotic-giant-branch stars are major sources of carbon, secondary nitrogen, and roughly half of the slow-neutron-capture (s-process) elements, on mass-dependent delays; the r-process requires a distinct high-neutron-flux site.
The nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio shows a low-metallicity plateau near log(N/O) approximately -1.6 (primary nitrogen) rising steeply at high oxygen abundance (secondary nitrogen).

Local star-forming disks show negative radial oxygen-abundance gradients (about -0.1 dex per effective radius) consistent with inside-out assembly, while stellar radial migration flattens and blurs stellar gradients over time.

Whether high [alpha/Fe] is a clean short-formation-timescale clock is debated, since a top-heavy IMF, metallicity-dependent yields, or burst timing could raise [alpha/Fe] independently of the star-formation history.
The supersolar N/O measured in GN-z11 at z = 10.6 is in tension with standard delayed nitrogen enrichment and has prompted competing explanations.

Whether z approximately 1-3 disks have steeper, flat, or inverted radial metallicity gradients is unresolved, as observed gradients are diverse and may reflect genuine cold-flow accretion or beam-smearing and geometry.

sections.section: The Cosmic Baryon and Metal Cycle

claims.text: More than about 90% of present-day baryons are gaseous rather than locked in stars, and the total baryon density (Omega_b approximately 0.0455) is concordant between Big-Bang nucleosynthesis and the CMB.

The cosmic neutral-atomic-hydrogen density Omega_HI evolves only weakly from z approximately 5 to 0, while the cosmic molecular-gas density rises to a peak near cosmic noon and declines, tracking the star-formation-rate density.
Only about 20-25% of the metals a galaxy has produced are retained in its stars, ISM, and dust; the majority reside in the circumgalactic medium or have been expelled.

There is no severe global missing-metals problem in the modern census: metals in cold (T < 10^4 K) gas at z > 2.5 approach the expected produced amount, and submillimeter galaxies contribute less than about 15% of the cosmic metal budget.
Both the dust-to-gas and dust-to-metals ratios decrease toward lower metallicity.
Whether Omega_HI is genuinely near-constant or biased by column-density thresholds and dust obscuration of high-column damped systems is debated.
The cosmic H2 density inferred from CO luminosity functions depends on excitation and the metallicity-dependent CO-to-H2 conversion, so its amplitude and peak redshift are uncertain.

Simulations can match integrated baryon and metal totals while assigning them to different temperatures, ionization states, and radii than observations imply, and CGM/LLS ionization corrections are model-dependent.
The circumgalactic medium (disk radius < r <= virial radius) is multiphase, spanning cold photoionized gas, warm transition gas, and hot coronal plasma along single sightlines.
Cool neutral/low-ionized hydrogen is ubiquitous out to about 150 kpc around both star-forming and passive L* galaxies.

Strong O VI absorption surrounds star-forming L* galaxies but is markedly weaker around passive ones, a dichotomy reproduced in simulations where the O VI peak coincides with the L* halo virial temperature.
The cool CGM holds a large ionized-gas reservoir, about 6.5e10 to 9.2 +/- 4.3e10 solar masses for L* galaxies, comparable to the galaxy's ISM, as found by two independent photoionization analyses.

Hot X-ray coronae are detected around only a handful of very massive spirals and fall well short of closing the baryon budget (the Milky Way hot halo is <= (0.5-1.5)e10 solar masses, only 2-5% of the missing baryons).

Low-ionization metal absorption is statistically concentrated along galaxy minor axes (biconical outflows) while co-rotating absorption aligns with the major axis (accretion); dust is also detected in the CGM.

Whether cool CGM clouds are rapidly shredded by Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities or survive and grow via cooling, conduction suppression, and thermal-instability precipitation (t_cool/t_ff <~ 10) is contested.
Whether O VI arises in ~10^5.5 K collisionally ionized gas or in photoionized/non-equilibrium cooling interfaces and turbulent mixing layers is unresolved.
claims.debate_topic: Origin of O VI and intermediate ions

claims.text: A bimodal cool-CGM metallicity distribution has been read as separating pristine accretion from enriched recycled outflows, but mixing and ionization overlap blur the interpretation.
claims.debate_topic: CGM metallicity as an origin tag

claims.text: Different wind prescriptions yield different CGM column densities and phase masses, so CGM observables constrain feedback only within model assumptions.

sections.section: Structural Evolution and Feedback in Galaxy-Formation Models

claims.text: Galaxy formation proceeds in two stages, collisionless dark-matter halo assembly followed by dissipative gas cooling, within the Lambda-CDM hierarchy.
Without feedback, gas cools catastrophically (overcooling), overproducing central mass and stars and losing angular momentum; this failure mode motivates all feedback prescriptions.
Cosmological simulations cannot resolve star formation and feedback directly and must use subgrid recipes calibrated to observed relations.

A supernova remnant transfers energy and momentum through free-expansion, Sedov-Taylor, shell-formation, and momentum-conserving stages, injecting a terminal radial momentum of about 2-3e5 solar-mass km/s per event near n_H ~ 1 cm^-3.
Depositing supernova thermal energy at insufficient numerical resolution causes it to radiate away artificially (numerical overcooling), a core reason feedback is hard to model.

Stellar/supernova-driven outflows regulate low-mass galaxies and transport metals, with mass loading scaling inversely with halo circular velocity; ejected gas need not escape permanently, as galactic fountains recycle it.

High-redshift star-forming disks are turbulent, clumpy, and rotationally supported (sigma0 ~ 40-80 km/s, v_rot/sigma0 ~ 2-6); violent disk instabilities form giant (~10^8-10^9 solar-mass) clumps that can migrate to build bulges.

The galaxy size-mass relation evolves since z approximately 3 with star-forming and quiescent populations following different size evolution, and compact quiescent galaxies already exist at z approximately 2; baseline disk sizes trace halo angular momentum.

Whether spheroids and compact cores form mainly through mergers or through internal violent disk instabilities and secular evolution is unresolved, and morphology alone does not identify the quenching mechanism.
claims.debate_topic: Mergers vs internal processes for structural growth

claims.text: Whether the elevated velocity dispersions of cosmic-noon disks are powered by stellar feedback or by gravitational instability and accretion is contested.

Reproducing observed stellar masses, star-formation rates, and mass functions does not prove the underlying mechanism is correct: distinct subgrid implementations match the same calibrated statistics while diverging in secondary predictions.

Higher numerical resolution need not converge to the true feedback coupling if new resolved phases change the effective problem, so tuned population agreement is not physical validation; same-initial-condition multi-code tests are required.
